newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Strong media brands prevent info overload - Time.
newsitem.headline: Strong media brands prevent info overload - Time.

text.p: Harassed consumers fighting information overload will increasingly turn to trusted media brand names to filter and select news and information for them, a leading U.S. magazine publisher said on Thursday.

"I think we're seeing a flight to quality in information. And I believe that flight to quality will accelerate in the next few years," Time Inc president and CEO Don Logan told an international advertising conference in Amsterdam.

"Consumers are learning to distinguish between news sources. And in that process they and we are rediscovering the free-market solution to the entire problem of distinguishing value: the brand name," he said.

Logan said Time Inc -- part of media giant Time Warner Inc -- expected to maintain double-digit earnings growth by carefully managing and developing its magazine brands which include Time, Fortune, People and Sports Illustrated.

"The path to growth at our company is now very clear: it is to leverage the power of our established brand magazines to create new products...carefully targeted to specific audiences...that will stand out in the information flood."

Time for Kids, a classroom edition of Time Inc's flagship news magazine launched two years ago, now had 1.2 million customers while a Spanish-language edition of People would begin monthly publication soon after successful tests, he said.

Furthermore, a regular golf supplement distributed selectively to 500,000 readers of Sports Illustrated who were also keen golfers had enabled the magazine to sell an extra 500 advertising pages last year to golf equipment suppliers.
Logan said there was no question that magazines would hold their own despite the proliferation of new television channels and new media such as the Internet.
Time Inc runs its own web site called Pathfinder with electronic versions of all of its major magazines, but Logan said it was still far from profitable.
"As far as we're concerned, the jury is still out on how long it will take for the Internet to become a profitable medium for communicators -- and for advertisers."
But again, consumers were likely to seek out familiar brand names such as Sports Illustrated, he said, rather than download content from the many sites run by well-meaning amateurs.

Logan said advertisers and agencies had to adapt to ensure that their message reached busy consumers who were bombarded with information from all sides. He said they needed to target specific audiences better and market products more personally.

"You know that the good old days of putting all your money into big TV network buys is not coming back. So plan now for a more complex age, when big reach must be cobbled together through an assortment of smaller vehicles."
"Under the umbrella of your big brand image campaign, begin developing a wider assortment of more targeted executions, tailored to more targeted audiences," he said.
